articles.title: Five signs an MVP has competing sources of truth
articles.meta_description: How to recognize when your MVP's frontend, backend, and data layers disagree — before scaling turns inconsistency into a business risk.
articles.author: AmirSaber Sharifi
articles.problem: Early MVPs often ship fast by letting each layer own its own version of state. That works until users, investors, or regulators start asking which number is correct.

sections.heading: Balances differ by surface
sections.body: The dashboard shows a balance the wallet API does not recognize, or the admin panel reports holdings the customer app never displays. When two screens answer the same question with different numbers, you have at least two sources of truth — not a display bug.

sections.heading: Event logs and application state diverge
sections.body: Your ledger or event stream says a transfer completed, but the product database still shows pending. Teams patch around this with retries and manual fixes instead of reconciling the model. That is a sign the write path was never unified.

sections.heading: On-chain reads disagree with backend APIs
sections.body: A wallet shows an active position while your indexer returns empty, or a contract state differs from what your API caches. In fintech and digital-asset products, this gap often means you are serving two authorities without a reconciliation layer.

sections.heading: Feature flags hide inconsistent behavior
sections.body: Different cohorts see different outcomes for the same action because each feature branch introduced its own persistence rules. Flags are useful for rollout — not for papering over incompatible data models.

sections.heading: Nobody can answer "what is the source of truth?"
sections.body: If engineering, product, and support each point to a different system when asked where the canonical record lives, you have an architecture problem — not a documentation gap. Fixing it gets harder after product-market fit.

articles.title: What a fractional principal architect fixes in the first 30 days
articles.meta_description: The first-month priorities when a fractional principal architect joins a seed–Series B company — boundaries, ownership, and decisions that compound.
articles.author: AmirSaber Sharifi
articles.problem: Founders hire fractional architecture leadership when delivery is stalling, costs are climbing, or the next funding round will scrutinize technical risk. The first 30 days should produce clarity — not another slide deck.

sections.heading: Map system boundaries and ownership
sections.body: The first deliverable is a shared map of services, data stores, and integration points — with named owners for each boundary. Ambiguous ownership is the most common root cause of slow delivery and recurring incidents.

sections.heading: Identify the single source of truth for core entities
sections.body: For each business-critical entity — user, account, balance, order, asset — the architect documents where the canonical record lives and how other systems derive their view. Competing sources of truth are resolved before new features add weight.

sections.heading: Prioritize the top three architectural risks
sections.body: Not every problem needs fixing in month one. A fractional principal ranks risks by business impact: security exposure, scaling ceilings, and dependencies that block the roadmap. The output is a sequenced plan founders can fund.

sections.heading: Establish design review for high-stakes changes
sections.body: A lightweight review gate for changes touching payments, custody, identity, or infrastructure cost. The goal is to catch irreversible decisions early — without slowing every pull request.

sections.heading: Align engineering and product on trade-offs
sections.body: The architect facilitates explicit trade-off conversations: build vs. buy, consistency vs. speed, build-out vs. hire. Founders get decision records they can share with investors and the board — not tribal knowledge locked in one engineer's head.
